html:
The Charrúa are an Indigenous people of the Southern Cone, in present Uruguay and nearby Entre Ríos in Argentina and Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil. They were seasonal nomads who lived by hunting deer and rhea, fishing and gathering.

In 1516 people of this coast killed the Spanish navigator Juan Díaz de Solís when he landed on the Río de la Plata. After horses spread across the plains in the 1600s the Charrúa became skilled horsemen and cattle raiders, and they fought Spanish and Portuguese settlers for two centuries. Many fought for the independence leader José Artigas. In 1831 the army of the new state of Uruguay lured them to a meeting at Salsipuedes Creek and massacred them. Four survivors were shipped to Paris and shown to the public. Their neighbours included the Guenoa and the Guaraní to the north.
